newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen rebel chief Basayev to run for president.
newsitem.headline: Chechen rebel chief Basayev to run for president.

text.p: One of rebel Chechnya's best known guerrilla commanders, Shamil Basayev, said on Friday he would stand for president of the region in elections next January and promised to crack down on crime if he won.
Basayev, who hijacked a aircraft to Turkey in 1991, became public enemy number one in Russia after leading a spectacular raid on the southern town of Budennovsk in June 1995.
A group of Chechen rebels under his command seized hostages in a hospital and over 100 people were killed.

But he became a hero in the rebel ranks after negotiating directly by telephone with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and escaping unpunished with his fellow fighters. The outcome was seen as a humiliation for the Kremlin.

The bearded rebel told reporters in Grozny: "Yes, I'm going to be president. I need power not for the sake of power but to fight crime which has swept over our republic and to ensure there is no corruption at the top."

Basayev defended his role in the Budennovsk raid, saying it should be balanced against Russian atrocities during the war, which lasted nearly two years and caused the deaths of tens of thousands of people.
"Before recalling Budennovsk, think about Grozny, Gudermes, Samashki and all the Chechen people who were killed. The action in Budennovsk was to force Russia to stop the war," he said.
Chechnya is now once again under the control of rebel fighters and elections will take place there on January 27.
Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev has already said he plans to run for the presidency.

Another possible candidate is acting premier Aslan Maskhadov, who commanded the guerrillas who beat off the Russian army, though he has so far shown loyalty to Yandarbiyev in order to avoid a split in separatist ranks.
Russia agreed last week to pull out its remaining troops from the region, paving the way for an agreement between the interim government in Grozny and the Kremlin.
Basayev said that once the Russian troops left there would be conditions for a free and fair election and internal conflicts on the Chechen side would subside.
"There are strong traditions in Chechnya based on democracy. There won't be a repetition of Afghanistan here, as some had wanted. We will be able to solve all our problems peacefully," he said.
Basayev's announcement came as the State Duma met in Moscow to debate the agreement signed last week between Maskhadov and Chernomyrdin.
Opposition parties say the agreement paves the way for the republic to secede from the Russian Federation and win full independence.
